did_you_know.text: Did you know? The words “statutes” and “judgments” refer to two kinds of instructions: rules that establish standards, and rulings connected with justice and law.
Did you know? Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, or for the mountain region where the Torah was given. Deuteronomy often uses the name “Horeb.”
Did you know? The biblical phrase “face to face” describes direct and close communication; it does not necessarily mean literally seeing a face.
Did you know? In the ancient world, people often made statues representing gods and worshiped them. This command forbids worshiping God through an image from the sky, the earth, or the waters.
Did you know? In the version of the commandments in Exodus, the Sabbath is introduced with “Remember,” while here it says “Observe.” The two words highlight different aspects of keeping the Sabbath.
Did you know? Sabbath rest is meant not only for free people, but also for servants, resident foreigners, and even animals. The Sabbath is therefore presented as a day with social significance.
Did you know? Here the Sabbath is explained as a reminder of the Exodus and freedom from slavery. In Exodus, by contrast, the Sabbath is connected with the story of creation.
Did you know? The verb “tirzah” is not the general Hebrew word for every kind of killing; it is mainly connected with forbidden killing. That is why many English translations use the word “murder.”
Did you know? The verse uses two different verbs: “covet” and “desire.” Both show that the commandments concern not only actions, but also a person’s inner desires.
Did you know? The phrase “Who would give” is a biblical way to express a wish or hope, not a question expecting an answer. Here it expresses God’s desire that the people continue on a good path.
